title: New York City’s 2026 Economic & Budget Outlook: Making Affordability a Reality Amidst Inequality and Fiscal Constraints
plain_title: The city's economic and budget outlook for 2026
what_they_audited: An annual outlook from the Center for New York City Affairs at The New School examining the city's economy, poverty and inequality, and the city and state budget picture heading into 2026, with recommendations for city and state policymakers.
background: The report says New York City is already the most economically unequal city in the country, and that federal actions in 2025, including the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), have added new strains to city and state budgets.

recommendations: Act now to retain every federal dollar, by decoupling New York tax law from the business tax changes in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and by investing in agency staffing, outreach and application systems so fewer people lose the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits or Medicaid under new work and reporting rules.
Use state reserve funds in state fiscal year 2027 for short-term, one-time investments that counteract the effect of federal actions on state and city programs.

Pass progressive city tax changes for fiscal year 2027, including adding higher personal income tax brackets, ending the Madison Square Garden property tax exemption, negotiating payments in lieu of taxes from large tax-exempt universities and hospitals, and pursuing comprehensive property tax reform.

Maintain existing core services and benefits programs, prioritize the administration of benefits as new federal requirements take effect, and uphold the city's sanctuary law while bolstering immigration legal services.
Pass laws that strengthen protections for workers against harms such as workplace injury and wage theft.
Establish and enforce higher labor standards in low-wage occupations, including phasing out the subminimum wage for tipped restaurant workers and further raising the state minimum wage.
Prioritize neighborhood small businesses and local job creation, including in infrastructure and climate resilience planning.
Direct state fiscal stimulus toward public works that create high-quality jobs, including zoning changes that spur private housing construction.
